first_impression.reaction: Typed 'prenup' on the train. I'm Australian, living in Singapore, and my fiance's family has property here, so it's on our list. The first line answers what it is in Australia and it's dated this month, so I kept going. Then the takeaways said the same thing again almost word for word. I jumped to 'who needs one', the overseas bit and the FAQ. Useful, but the middle is a wall of legal lists on a phone screen. Bookmarked for the overseas section.

journey.quote: In Australia, a prenup is a binding financial agreement, a contract made under Part VIIIA of the Family Law Act 1975 for married couples.
journey.reaction: Answer in the first line, good. Bit heavy with the Part VIIIA stuff for someone on a train, but I know what I'm looking at.

journey.quote: As at November 2026, it is only binding if it meets the technical requirements of the Act, and each of you must receive independent legal advice from an Australian lawyer before you sign.
journey.reaction: Dated and specific. That's the thing I'd have got wrong: two lawyers, not one.

journey.quote: The celebration itself is where [Wedded Concierge](https://weddedwonderland.com/wonderland-concierge?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=content&utm_campaign=prenup&utm_content=primary) comes in.
journey.reaction: A wedding planner plug on a legal page before I've hit the takeaways. One line, so I scroll past, but it feels a bit early.

journey.quote: In Australia a prenup is a binding financial agreement made under Part VIIIA of the Family Law Act 1975.
journey.reaction: I literally just read this. The takeaways repeat the intro instead of giving me something new, like who it suits or the overseas catch.

journey.quote: Treat the financial advice as Moneysmart's recommendation; the court and legal aid pages make independent legal advice the requirement.
journey.reaction: Helpful. Tells me what's must-do and what's nice-to-do.

journey.section: Why some prenups are set aside
journey.quote: Legal Aid NSW lists grounds that include: fraud (such as hiding important financial information); an agreement made to defeat a creditor; one made to cheat a de facto partner of one of the parties; the agreement being void or unenforceable; it no longer being practical to carry out all or part of it; a material change of circumstances affecting a child that causes hardship; unconscionable conduct; a payment flag on a party's superannuation; and dealing with a superannuation interest that cannot be split under the law.
journey.reaction: One giant sentence, then another long list from Victoria straight after that mostly says the same thing. On my phone this is where I started thumbing fast.

journey.quote: No source says a couple needs one.
journey.reaction: Odd way to open the section I actually came for. Sounds like a research note, not an answer. Just tell me who it usually suits.

journey.quote: Legal Aid NSW says an agreement can protect an inheritance a partner may receive in future.
journey.reaction: That's us, more or less. Short subheadings here are easy to scan.

journey.quote: An agreement made overseas is not automatically recognised in Australia and must meet the Australian formal requirements to be valid here.
journey.reaction: This is the line I needed. If we'd signed something in Singapore I'd have assumed it counted.

journey.section: How to get a prenup and when to sign before the wedding
journey.quote: How much lead time your agreement needs is a question for your lawyers, so raise it at the first meeting.
journey.reaction: The heading says 'when to sign before the wedding' and the answer is 'ask your lawyer'. I wanted at least a rough idea of how far ahead.

journey.section: Prenups for destination weddings and international couples
journey.quote: If you plan to sign in Australia and then marry overseas, ask your lawyer how the overseas ceremony affects your agreement.
journey.reaction: Fair, it's general info. But it's my exact question and it ends in another 'ask your lawyer'. At least I know what to ask.

journey.section: Prenups for destination weddings and international couples
journey.quote: The agreement stays with your lawyers. The celebration is different work: one Wedded Advisor plans the venue, travel and vendors with you as a single point of contact, anywhere in the world, through [Wedded Concierge](https://weddedwonderland.com/wonderland-concierge?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=content&utm_campaign=prenup&utm_content=secondary).
journey.reaction: Honest that they don't touch the legal side. 'Anywhere in the world' is interesting since we might marry in Bali.

journey.quote: No. You cannot enter into a financial agreement without each first getting independent legal advice from an Australian lawyer.
journey.reaction: Straight yes/no answers. This FAQ is the best part for a quick read.

journey.quote: Yes. An agreement can be made during the marriage or after it.
journey.reaction: Takes the pressure off if we run out of time before the wedding.

unanswered_questions: Roughly how far before the wedding should we start if we want it signed beforehand?
If I'm Australian and my partner isn't, and we live in Singapore, does the Australian agreement still matter for us?
Does marrying overseas, say in Bali, change anything if we sign in Australia first?
Does Wedded Wonderland work with couples who live outside Australia?

turn_offs_found.quote: In Australia a prenup is a binding financial agreement made under Part VIIIA of the Family Law Act 1975.
turn_offs_found.why: The Key Takeaways repeat the intro almost line for line, so the box I rely on to decide whether to stay gives me nothing new. One takeaway on who it suits and one on overseas agreements would have hooked me faster.

turn_offs_found.quote: No source says a couple needs one.
turn_offs_found.why: It's the section I searched for and it opens like a footnote. It reads as hedging rather than a plain answer, and makes the page feel less confident.

turn_offs_found.quote: How much lead time your agreement needs is a question for your lawyers, so raise it at the first meeting.
turn_offs_found.why: The heading promises 'when to sign before the wedding', and the body doesn't say. Headings that don't match the answer make me stop trusting the rest of the headings.

turn_offs_found.quote: [Victoria Legal Aid](https://www.legalaid.vic.gov.au/agreement-about-dividing-property) says financial agreements are legally binding unless it can be proved that: there was fraud; the agreement is not practical; it did not follow the formal requirements under the Family Law Act; there has been a major and unexpected change affecting a child; one person acted in an unfair way; one person did not follow the agreement; or property covered was taken by the government because of criminal activity.
turn_offs_found.why: Second long run-on list straight after a near-identical one. On a phone that's a solid block of semicolons, and it's where I nearly left.

would_share_with: My fiance, for the overseas agreement point and the 'two lawyers' rule
A friend in Sydney with kids from a first marriage, for the blended families bit

cta_reaction.quote: Your Wedded Advisor plans the venue, travel and vendors with you, with the fee agreed in writing before any work begins.
cta_reaction.why: I came for prenup info, not a planner. But the plugs stayed short, they're clear they don't do the legal side, and 'fee agreed in writing' sounds above board. If we go with Bali I might come back.

top_3_changes: Rewrite the Key Takeaways so they add something beyond the intro, for example who it commonly suits and that an overseas agreement isn't automatically recognised in Australia.

Open 'Who needs a prenup?' with a plain answer (no one is required to have one; it often suits couples with property, inheritances, children from earlier relationships or assets across countries) instead of 'No source says a couple needs one.'
Merge the two set-aside lists into one short bulleted list of common grounds, and make the 'when to sign before the wedding' heading match what the section can actually say.
